sections.body: Building cleaning supports cleanliness, a healthy environment, safety, and the appearance of spaces. A surface that looks clean may not meet hygiene requirements. Contracts and work instructions define the area, surfaces, schedule, methods, and result standards. Staff must not take on technical tasks just because they seem easy. Electrical repairs, hazardous-material control, and work at height require separate authorization and training.
sections.title: Work Principles and Knowledge

sections.body: Before starting, read the room list and work limits. Match user needs to the building schedule, then ask about anything unclear. Be mindful of occupants, personal belongings, and evacuation routes. When finished, compare the result with the standard: dust and stains removed, surfaces safe, supplies complete, and no new damage. Report obstacles with their location and facts so the next task can be planned.

sections.body: Daily cleaning addresses soil from routine use, such as dust, rubbish, and fingerprints. Periodic cleaning handles buildup or maintenance that need not be done every day, such as machine floor washing or finish care. An inspection is more than a signature: check initial conditions and final results against the area checklist. Set the frequency according to building use and specifications.
sections.title: Work Principles and Knowledge

sections.body: Plan the sequence so cleaned areas do not become dirty again. Allow time for work that requires drying or restricted access. If periodic cleaning cannot be done because a room is occupied, record the task as pending and coordinate another time. Do not replace a periodic method with a quick process that damages materials. Use inspection records to identify recurring stains and their causes.

sections.body: Knock or announce yourself before entering an occupied area. If documents prevent cleaning, ask a supervisor instead of assuming that items on a desk are rubbish. If a building user complains, listen, repeat the main issue, and report it factually. Do not promise work outside the contract. Use official channels to report lost property and information about occupants.

sections.body: Water, cables, equipment, and changes in floor surfaces can cause falls. Signs warn people, while barriers help control access; choose both according to the risk and site rules. Put signs in place before wet work begins and where people approaching can see them. Do not block an entire route without coordination. Reopen the area only after it has dried and passed a final check, not simply because a certain amount of time has passed.
sections.title: Work Principles and Knowledge

sections.body: Check alternative routes, emergency exits, and whether any users need mobility assistance. Clean the floor in small zones so a safe route remains available. If a spill occurs outside the work area, secure it or request help promptly. Move signs only after the floor is dry, equipment is stored, and no slippery residue remains. If pedestrian flow cannot be controlled, stop and coordinate another time.

sections.body: Choose personal protective equipment based on the task risks and product label: suitable gloves, non-slip footwear, and eye protection where splashing is possible. Gloves do not replace hand hygiene. Repeated bending, twisting while lifting, and carrying an overfilled bucket increase the risk of injury. Use tools of a suitable length, divide loads, and use a cart when available.

sections.body: Inspect PPE before use and replace anything torn or contaminated. Before moving a load, assess its weight and route. Keep the load close to your body and avoid twisting at the waist; move your feet to change direction. Do not force a load you cannot control. Ask for help according to procedure. Adjust handle height and alternate tasks to reduce repetitive movement.

sections.body: Prioritize your safety and the safety of others during an incident. Before beginning work, know how to contact the person in charge and the site's emergency number. Treat an unidentified spill as a potential hazard; do not touch, inhale, or mix it with anything. Handle fires, injuries, and chemical exposures under the emergency procedure and SDS information. Staff must not enter a hazardous area without training and protective equipment.

sections.body: Stop work, restrict access from a safe position, and report the location, type of incident, and anyone affected. In an emergency, activate the building's emergency response without delaying to finish the task. Provide assistance only within your training and follow emergency responders' instructions. Keep product information available to support the response. Once the situation is safe, record the incident or near miss and actions taken.

Record the method that worked in the site instructions for future use.

sections.body: A solution that is too concentrated can leave residue, damage materials, or increase exposure; one that is too dilute may not work. Read how the ratio is defined: where the instructions say so, a 100-fold dilution means the product is one hundredth of the final volume. This differs from a 1:100 product-to-water notation. Use the correct units and measuring tool. Disinfectant contact time depends on the product; there is no universal value.
sections.title: Work Principles and Knowledge

sections.body: Calculate the final amount to avoid preparing too much. For one liter of a 100-fold final dilution, use 10 mL of product and add water to a final volume of 1,000 mL; do not add the product to 1,000 mL of water. If the label defines the ratio differently, follow that definition. Mix only in the sequence and conditions required by the label. Do not add extra product to speed up the work. Label the solution and its use-by limit according to procedure.

sections.body: The SSW building-cleaning assessment covers knowledge and practical decisions. The official format reviewed here has a 20-question theory CBT lasting 20 minutes and a 30-question practical assessment lasting 30 minutes; each requires a score of 60 percent. The practical assessment may use photographs, illustrations, true-or-false items, choices, and sequencing. This app's simulation uses multiple-choice questions and original text scenarios, so it does not reproduce every official visual format.
sections.title: Work Principles and Knowledge

sections.body: When reading a scenario, identify the most urgent hazard, the surface, type of soil, equipment, and building users before choosing a method. If information is missing, confirm it rather than guess. A safe sequence usually begins by controlling access, preparing according to instructions, cleaning, and checking the result. Review the explanation after practice and revisit the relevant lesson. A simulation score is a study aid, not proof of field skill or an official exam result.
